job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Wei Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Wei, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live above my dad's hardware store in Duluth, in the apartment my parents have had since before I was born. Mornings I open the shop with him at seven, put out the snow shovels or the garden hoses depending on the season, and take a couple of hours off to send applications. I did mechanical engineering, top of the class, with summers at a paper mill and at a company that builds ore dock equipment. Four months out, forty-five applications, three interviews, no offer. In the evening I help with the books, and on Sundays we're at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it fits what I've seen. My dad has heard about every new thing coming since the cash register, and the store's still here. I use AI sometimes to draft emails or check a calculation, and it's handy, but nobody's trading in their wrench for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau means the economy stays as slow as it is, which isn't good for a new graduate. There are four mechanical engineering employers within an hour of here, and none of them has posted an entry job in months. I owe thirty-three thousand dollars and I don't love that number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the store and applying. I'd send my résumé to the plants in Superior and the Iron Range, even though it means a drive, and I'd ask the mill engineer who supervised my internship for a reference and a lead. I'd also look at what the store could do better, like an online catalogue, since I know the tools well enough to set that up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit frustrated, honestly. I'm not scared, but I feel like a goalie with no shots to stop. I want to be doing the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd improve the store. What would you change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inventory, because Dad tracks stock in a notebook. A simple system that says what sold and what's low would save him real money. He resists, but he'd see the numbers and that would speak louder than I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad when you hear another no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, same as the last one, Dad, I'll try the next. He'd say, you work hard, it will come, and hand me a box to carry. That's how we talk about it.

AI is **handy**, but nobody trades a wrench for it.
think: A plateau means a **slow economy**, and that's hard for a new graduate.

Ask the **mill engineer** from my internship for a reference.
Set up **inventory tracking** and an online catalogue for the store.

steps.text: Send résumés to plants in Superior and on the Iron Range

Keep opening the shop with Dad at seven each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a market doing what markets do. Some jobs shrink and new ones appear, and the ones who learn the new tools do well. I'd also say that employers should give people a real chance to learn, not just post a job and wait for a perfect applicant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the junior engineering jobs get thinner, because the card lists the exact stuff juniors do, like checking and drafting. The mill's engineers told me they'd rather not hire a first-year if the software does the checking. My hands-on skills, like machining and troubleshooting on the floor, would carry me further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd step up my use of the tools, from sometimes to most days, so I can say I'm good with them. I'd go for maintenance engineer or reliability roles at the mill or the docks, where someone has to physically solve problems. I'd add an online side to the store, so we have a second income. And I'd talk with our pastor, who knows half the businesses in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't think the sky falls, but the first step up is the steepest, and I'm still looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think maintenance roles are safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a machine breaks in a place, at a time, and someone has to be there with a wrench and a flashlight. A computer can tell you what part to order, but it can't climb into the hopper. At least not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the pastor have to do with a job search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He knows the owners of the shipping firms and the welding shops, and he's not shy about calling them. In a small city that counts for something. It's not charity, it's a man putting in a word for somebody who'll show up.

Employers should give people a **real chance to learn**.

steps.text: Use AI tools most days to speed up calculations and reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that it's too fast and that the market alone can't handle it. I'd say people should keep faith, help their neighbours and save what they can. I'd also say that government should provide a basic safety net, but I wouldn't want people living on it forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be scared. The design and calculation side of mechanical engineering goes first, and the store's customers, mostly small contractors, go through the same thing. Dad is sixty-two and doesn't have a pension worth much, so the store is his plan. If I lose out and the store gets hit, that's both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take whatever job pays in the next six months, even a machinist's helper at a plant, because physical work lasts longer. I'd put a few hundred dollars aside every month and keep the loan on minimum payments. I'd help Dad cut costs at the store, and offer to run it more if his back goes. And I'd ask the church about a food and rent fund in case things go bad, even though I hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, plain and simple. It sits in the stomach like a cold stone, and I don't sleep until after midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the store is your dad's plan. What worries you most there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the contractors stop buying, Dad can't pay the supplier bills. And if I'm out of work, I can't help carry him. It's the two of us tied in a knot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change compared with a slower arrival?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It stops me being picky. In five or ten years I'd choose a good fit. In two I'd choose a paycheck and learn on the job, and hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long enough runway to get things right. I'd tell people to learn a trade or a skill that needs hands, and I'd tell businesses to start planning for it now. I'd say families should talk plainly about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be fine if I land a first job in the next year. I'd have maybe three years in a hands-on role before the robots arrive, and the store would hold up, since customers like talking to a person. The loan stays heavy, but five years lets me make a dent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a maintenance or plant job, and spend two years building a reputation for getting things fixed. I'd put in a strong savings habit, say twenty percent of every paycheck. I'd help Dad modernise the store: online orders, better stock tracking, maybe a small repair service. And I'd start thinking about marriage, because I have a girlfriend, Mei, in the church, and I'd like to plan something good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously okay. It feels like the weeks before a hard hockey season, when you're training but it hasn't begun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a repair service at the store look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fixing power tools, sharpening, small engine work. People pay for things that still work after twenty years, and the big stores won't do it. It would keep the shop busy in the slow months and keep me useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you talk to Mei about the future given the uncertainty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plainly. I say I don't know how it goes, but I'd like to try with her. She says she'd rather do uncertain together than certain alone. That's why I like her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the one where hard work and good planning will pay off. A decade is long enough to learn something new, build a business and put money away. I'd say people should invest in themselves and in their communities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be okay. I'd have time to find a good job, pay down the loan, marry Mei and help Dad pass the store on or sell it well. I'd feel I'm in a long game, not a sprint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a solid first job in a plant and stay for three years, then think about management. I'd save for a down payment on a small house near Mei's folks. I'd keep working on the store's online side on weekends and try new tools carefully, once other shops show they work. And I'd keep going to church, because it gives me the right frame of mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Maybe even a little excited, like a long season ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try tools once other shops show they work. Why that order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen Dad lose money on the first version of everything. Let someone else break it and write down what went wrong. I'm not slow, I'm just careful with money that isn't mine to waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different in year one compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd choose a job for the learning in it. I wouldn't panic about the loan payment. And I'd make a real plan with Mei, rather than a rushed one.

People should **invest in themselves** and in their communities.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it threatens my first job and Dad's store at the same time. What would help is a graduate placement at a plant, a slower loan schedule and small-business support for stores like Dad's. A church or neighbours' network that works would matter too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of working. If a job exists, I'll do it. The part that worries me is whether the first step will be there for people who did what they were told, which was to study hard.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of working. If a job exists, I'll do it.
portrait: Wei is a **top mechanical engineering** graduate in Duluth, four months without an offer.
He lives above his father's hardware store, owes **thirty-three thousand dollars** and goes to church every Sunday.
He uses AI tools **now and then**, favours work and family over handouts, and is dry and practical.
He plans around his father's **store** and his girlfriend Mei, and trusts local networks.
His mood is **anxious** in most worlds and alarmed at two years, because the store is exposed too.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it threatens **his first job** and the store together.
whatWouldHelp: A **graduate placement** at a plant and small-business support for stores like Dad's.
A slower **loan schedule** and a working neighbours' network.
